tip: Being careful or alert uses 'stare', not 'essere': 'stai attento'.
'Amico' has an irregular plural, 'amici', pronounced with a soft 'c'.
Health and how you feel use 'stare', not 'essere': 'stiamo benissimo'.
Informal 'tu' commands of '-ere' and '-ire' verbs use the present tense form: 'bevi' = drink.
Italian often uses the present tense for scheduled future events: 'partite domani' = you leave tomorrow.
'Dire' is irregular; the 'noi' form is 'diciamo', not 'dicamo'.
'Lo' and 'la' shorten to 'l'' before a vowel: 'l'acqua'.
Verbs ending in '-gare' add an 'h' before an ending starting with 'i', keeping the hard 'g': 'paghiamo'.
Feminine 'una' becomes 'un'' before a vowel: 'un'insalata'. Masculine 'un' never takes an apostrophe.
'Autobus' is invariable: 'l'autobus' is singular, 'gli autobus' plural, spelled the same.
'Chiamarsi' is reflexive; 'ti chiami' literally means you call yourself.
Age uses 'avere', not 'essere': 'quanti anni hai?' asks how many years you have.
'Aspettare' already means to wait for, so no 'per' follows it: 'aspetti l'autobus'.
'Da' plus 'l'' contracts to 'dall'': 'dall'autobus'.
An adjective agrees with its noun: 'ragazza' is feminine, so tall becomes 'alta', ending in '-a'.
Adjectives ending in '-e' use one form for both genders: 'pesante' for masculine or feminine.
Italian usually uses the article, not a possessive, for body parts: 'i capelli' = her hair.
'Arancione' ends in '-e', so it changes only for number: 'arancioni' in the plural, either gender.
'Bere' has an irregular past participle, 'bevuto', not 'beruto'.
Verbs taking 'essere' make the participle agree with the subject: 'siamo caduti' ends in '-i' to match we.
Yes/no questions usually keep normal word order; rising tone marks them in speech: 'Hai pagato il conto?'
The past tense uses helper verb 'avere' plus a participle: 'hai chiamato' = you called.
'Abbastanza' means enough, never changes form, and sits before the noun: 'abbastanza soldi'.
'Magari' plus a past subjunctive expresses a wish: 'magari smettesse' = if only it would stop.
Possessives normally take the definite article: 'la mia macchina', literally the my car.
Form comparatives by putting 'più' before the adjective: 'più leggera' = lighter.
Before an adjective 'molto' means very and never changes form: 'molto dolce'.
'Suonare' is the verb for playing instruments: 'suonare il pianoforte'. Games use 'giocare'.
'Palazzo' usually means a building or apartment block, not a palace.
After a time expression, 'fa' means ago: 'due giorni fa' = two days ago.
